                       LINK N3 OPPOSITION LANDOWNERS’ REPLY BRIEF

           Link N3 Opposition Landowners files this Reply Brief. Pursuant to SOAH Order No. 32,

  addressing post-hearing matters, this Reply Brief is timely filed on or before June 26, 2026. Along

  with this Reply Brief, the Link N3 Opposition Landowners incorporate by reference the reply brief

  of Save the Lampasas, 25, Inc. (Save the Lampasas).1


                                          I.    EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

           This Reply Brief advocates for the use of Links N4 or N12 rather than Link N3 in the

  western portion of the Study Area by showing how selected routes that use those links better

  address the routing criteria. This Reply Brief does this by showing the following:




           1
             Similar to the initial brief, for the purposes of judicial economy, the Link N3 Opposition Landowners
  incorporate by reference all the arguments made by Save the Lampasas in its reply brief. As the Link N3 Opposition
  Landowners are on the western half of the Study Area near the existing Big Hill substation, it files a separate brief to
  address arguments that focus on concerns related to the Link N3 Opposition Landowners.
                                                                                               Page 3 of 17


           The routing analysis is a balancing act, and no route is superior in all the routing criteria,
            but Routes 296, 572, and CCG are all superior in addressing the routing criteria than
            Route 894;

           Routes 296, 572, and CCG all exhibit superior performance in paralleling existing
            infrastructure;

           All of the routes are within a very small cost range – from approximately 0.22 to 4%
            more expensive than Route 894;

           Routes 296, 572, and CCG cross the Colorado River using existing compatible
            infrastructure rather than utilizing undisturbed property;

           All of the routes perform similarly regarding the length of route across areas of high
            archeological/historical site potential; and

           Routes that use Link N12, including Route 392 and 894 Western Mod 1, better address
            aesthetics by routing the transmission line near existing wind turbines.

   This Reply Brief also responds to the initial briefs of the Florence Independent School District,

the Yates Keith Alliance, Mark Allen Bradbury, the Gainer Family, and Austin C. and Janet Rose,

in their respective sections.


                                       II.    INTRODUCTION

        On March 26, 2026, Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission

Service (collectively, Joint Applicants) filed an application (Application) with the Public Utility

Commission of Texas (Commission) to amend its certificate of convenience and necessity for the

proposed Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kilovolt (kV) transmission line

project in Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell, Lampasas, Llano, Mason, McCulloch, Menard, Milam,

Mills, San Saba, Schleicher, Tom Green, and Williamson Counties.

        On June 19, 2026, the Link N3 Opposition Landowners filed its Initial Brief arguing that

the use of Link N4 or N12 in the western half of the Study Area is superior to the use of N3 based
                                                                                                    Page 4 of 17


on the Commission’s routing criteria found in PURA § 37.056 and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B).2

The Link N3 Opposition Landowners continue to assert this is the case and uses this Reply Brief

to demonstrate that routes utilizing N4 or N12 are better choices based on the routing criteria than

the best meets route, Route 894. Overall, the Link N3 Opposition Landowners will demonstrate

that Routes 296, 572, and CCG are better choices when considering the routing criteria and should

be chosen by the Commission over Route 894 and other routes that utilize Link N3.

        As discussed in the Initial Brief, two routing combinations exist to replace N3 in the central

corridor: N3  M5-N4-O3 and N3  N2-N11-N12.3 Routes that use the link combination M5-

N4-O3 include Route 296 and CCG.4 Route 572 uses the southern corridor on the eastern half of

the Study Area, but is similar in its substitution of N3  M4-N4-O3.5 Lastly, Route 392 utilizes

the northern corridor throughout the study area and uses Link N12.6

        Overall, there is no perfect route, and the selection of a route is based on a balancing act.

However, as discussed in detail with this brief, routes that utilize N4 or N12 including Route 296,

CCG, and 572 better address the routing criteria than Route 894 through a balancing of the routing

factors. For instance, Route CCG has greater paralleling within existing corridors,7 avoids the

Florence Elementary School at Link F348 as well as problematic Colorado River and San Saba

                                         III.     ROUTING CRITERIA

        A.          Paralleling

paralleling existing ROW of transmission lines and highways.20 In comparison, of all four routes

        Furthermore, Routes 572, 296, and CCG all use paralleling of existing compatible

infrastructure for the Colorado River crossing rather than crossing undisturbed property at Link

J22.22 Route 296, 572, and CCG all cross the Colorado River at Link J31, which parallels an

existing pipeline corridor.23 Paralleling existing transmission lines or highways was an important

community value expressed by landowners in the Study Area from the comments/questionnaires

received at the public participation meetings.24

        Overall, Routes 296, 296, and CCG better utilize existing compatible ROW, a factor

considered by 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(i) and (ii).

        B.       Prudent Avoidance

        Routes 296, CCG, and 572 all have either 105 or107 habitable structures within 500 feet

of the route centerline, well within a reasonable range for this length of transmission line.25 As

noted by some parties in their initial briefs, Route 392 has 136 habitable structures within 500 feet

of the route centerline,26 but what is not noted is that 19 of those habitable structures are on Link

U3, which as noted above parallels an existing transmission line for most of its length.27

        Florence Independent School District’s issue regarding the routing of the proposed

transmission line along Link F3 (on Route 296) was the potential health effects for the students at

        D.        Cultural, Aesthetic, and Historical Values

        The Yates Keith Alliance argues that routes 296 and 572 should not be chosen by the

Commission due to cultural resources located on those routes and advocates for the selection of

Route 894.39 Additionally, the initial brief of Mark Allen Bradbury argues that the Commission

should reject the selection of routes using the N2-N11-N12-P1 corridor due to cultural resource

site crossings.40

        First, the Yates Keith Alliance argues that the Joint Applicants data table assigned zero

recorded cultural resources crossed by Link G6 and zero recorded cultural resources within 1,000

feet of Link G6.41 However, as noted in Rose Exhibit 2, the Texas Historical Commission assigned

Trinomial 41B2562 in December 2025 and the entire property was not marked until March 2026,

the same month this application was filed with the Commission.42 As noted by the EA, “the overall

site density and diversity indicate high archeological sensitivity within the project area and support

the likelihood of encountering additional unrecorded cultural resources.”43 Therefore, it is likely

that additional cultural sites will be discovered as this transmission line process moves forward.

This is further substantiated the Joint Applicants data table having similar values for the routes

        E.         Environmental Integrity

        Environmental Integrity for this proceeding focuses mostly on the Colorado River and San

Saba Rivers.

                      1.      Colorado River

        Each of the following routes crosses the Colorado River at different links. As explained by

Mr. Rae Lynn Reinecke, “[t]he Colorado River serves as [a] major hydrologic and biological

corridor through the broader region. Portions of the river provide USFWS-designated critical

habitat for species listed and proposed under the ESA and are recognized by TWPD as ESSS.”50

        Routes 296, 572, and CCG all cross the Colorado River at Link J31.51 While Link J31 is

part of the central corridor, Link J31 would parallel an existing pipeline corridor instead of

undisturbed property.52 Link J31 is recommended by Ms. Reinecke as the Colorado River crossing

“given the ESSS avoidance, proximity to public parks, and infrastructure consolidation

                            IV.     SUMMARY OF ROUTING CRITERIA

       A.        Link Level Summary

       As discussed in the Initial Brief, Link N4 and Link N12 are better choices for routing than

Link N3.70 The use of Link N4 and Link N12 cost less per mile than using Link N3, better parallels

existing infrastructure through the use of Links O3 and N11, and better addresses community

values and aesthetics through the use of Link N12, which is near existing wind turbines and not

undisturbed property.71

       B.        Routing Level Summary

       As discussed above, Routes 296, CCG, and 572address the routing criteria better than

Route 894, which contains Link N3. Route 894 only marginally performs better in two instances:

cost and prudent avoidance.72 However, it excels in those two criteria at a detriment to

environmental integrity. Route 894 crosses the Colorado River at a location that would be directly

within view of Colorado Bend and Forest Bend State Parks and 4,000 feet away from the highly
